s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the two early censuses of British India?
o: The first census was synchronous in 1881, while the first non-synchronous census was held in 1901.
The first census was synchronous in 1872 and the first non-synchronous census was in 1881.
The first census was non-synchronous in 1872, while the first synchronous census was held in 1881.
Both the first census and the first synchronous census were held in 1872.
x: The census conducted under Mayo in 1872 was the first, but it was non-synchronous. The first synchronous census was held in 1881 during Lord Ripon's tenure.

s: Who assassinated Lord Mayo in the Andamans in 1872?
x: Mayo was killed by the convict Sher Ali Afridi in the Andamans in 1872; Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal threw a bomb at Hardinge II.

s:
Consider the following statements about Lord Canning:
1. His tenure was 1856–1862.
2. He was the last Governor-General under the Company and the first Viceroy under the Crown.
3. The Allahabad High Court was established in 1866 during his tenure.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
x: Canning served 1856–1862 as the last Company Governor-General and first Crown Viceroy; his term ended before the Allahabad High Court came in 1866.

s: During whose tenure was the portfolio system introduced?
x: Canning's tenure saw the Indian Councils Act 1861, the portfolio system, the first universities and the IPC.

s: Which Viceroy is correctly matched with his tenure?
x: Lawrence served 1864–1869; Canning 1856–1862, Mayo 1869–1872 and Lytton 1876–1880.

s: Who declared Shimla the summer capital of British India in 1864?
x: Sir John Lawrence declared Shimla the summer capital in 1864 (APPSC 2018 key). Canning was Viceroy until 1862. Mayo came in 1869 and is known for financial decentralisation. Lytton held the 1877 Durbar.

s: With which viceroyalty is the Wahabi movement associated?
x: Elgin I (1862-63) faced the Wahabi movement; Elgin II faced famine and plague in 1896-97.

s: Which Viceroy abolished income tax?
x: Northbrook (1872-76) abolished income tax; Canning had introduced it.

s: With which Viceroy are Rajkot College and the Department of Agriculture and Commerce associated?
x: Mayo founded Mayo College (Ajmer) and Rajkot College and set up the Department of Agriculture and Commerce.

s: Which Governor-General is associated with the Third Anglo-Burmese War and the last major territorial expansion?
x: Lord Dufferin (1884 to 1888) fought the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885, which annexed Upper Burma as the last major territorial expansion.

s: Under which Viceroy was the Indian Forest Department set up?
x: John Lawrence (1864-69) set up the Indian Forest Department and made Shimla the summer capital.

s: Which Viceroy mocked the Indian National Congress as representing a 'microscopic minority'?
x: Dufferin, in whose time the INC was founded (1885), called it a 'microscopic minority'.

s: During whose tenure was the Indian Councils Act of 1861, under which three Indians were nominated to the Viceroy's Legislative Council, passed?
x: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 was passed during Lord Canning's tenure. The nominated Indians included the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.

s: Which of the following was NOT one of the three Indians nominated under the Indian Councils Act, 1861?
x: The three Indians nominated in 1861 were the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.

s: In which year did Mayo's Resolution begin financial decentralisation?
x: Mayo's Resolution of 14 December 1870 began financial decentralisation.

s: In which year was Lord Lytton's Royal Titles Act passed?
x: The Royal Titles Act came in 1876, after Mayo's 1870 resolution and before Ripon's 1881 Factory Act.

s: With which of the following is the term 'Magna Carta of Local Self-Government' associated?
o: Financial decentralisation resolution of Lord Mayo
Local Self-Government Resolution of Lord Ripon
Indian Councils Act of Lord Lansdowne
x: Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882 is described as the Magna Carta of Local Self-Government. Ripon is consequently called the Father of Local Self-Government.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Lord Northbrook — Abolition of income tax
x: The Second Factory Act was passed under Lord Lansdowne in 1891, not Ripon; the other three pairs are correct.

s: Which of the following developments contributed to the growth of early nationalism during Lord Lytton's tenure?
o: The establishment of the Archaeological Survey of India
The holding of a Durbar during famine conditions along with the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act
The introduction of elected local bodies and financial autonomy
The appointment of the Royal Commission on Labour
x: Lytton's reactionary policies, including the Durbar during famine conditions, the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act, fuelled early nationalist criticism.

s: To what age did Lytton reduce the maximum age for the ICS examination from 21?
x: Lytton cut the ICS age from 21 to 19.

s: During whose viceroyalty was the Arms Act of 1878 passed?
x: Lytton passed the Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act in 1878.

s: Under which Viceroy was the Second Factory Act (1891) passed?
x: Lansdowne passed the Second Factory Act (1891); the first Factory Act (1881) was under Ripon.

s: Which British Prime Minister's Liberal government sent Lord Ripon to India?
x: Ripon was sent by Gladstone's Liberal government; Lytton had been appointed by Disraeli.

s: The European agitation against the Ilbert Bill (1883) is known as:
x: The European protest against Ripon's Ilbert Bill was called the 'White Mutiny'.

s: What title did Queen Victoria take at the Delhi Durbar of 1877?
x: At Lytton's Delhi Durbar of 1 January 1877 Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India (Kaiser-i-Hind).

s: What did the controversy surrounding the Ilbert Bill expose?
o: Racial discrimination in the colonial judicial system
The financial conflict between the central and provincial governments
The dispute over the Afghan boundary
The division between famine and irrigation administration
x: The Ilbert Bill controversy revealed the racial discrimination involved in preventing Indian judges from exercising jurisdiction over European British subjects on equal terms.

s: The First Factory Act (1881) banned the employment of children below what age?
x: The First Factory Act of 1881 under Ripon banned the employment of children below 7.

s:
Arrange in chronological order:
1. Ilbert Bill
2. Royal Titles Act
3. Indian Councils Act (Lansdowne)
4. Vernacular Press Act
x: Royal Titles Act (1876), Vernacular Press Act (1878), Ilbert Bill (1883), Indian Councils Act (1892).

s: On which date were the annulment of the Partition of Bengal and the transfer of the capital to Delhi announced at the Delhi Durbar?
x: Both, with the creation of Bihar and Orissa, were announced on 12 December 1911.

s: Under which Viceroy was Queen Victoria proclaimed Empress of India at the 1877 Delhi Durbar?
x: Lytton's 1877 Durbar proclaimed Victoria Empress (Kaiser-i-Hind).

s: Whose coronation did the Delhi Durbar of 1911 mark?
x: The 1911 Durbar marked the coronation of George V and Queen Mary; the 1903 Durbar was for Edward VII.

s: Under which Viceroy was the Delhi Durbar of 1903, for the coronation of Edward VII, held?
x: Curzon held the 1903 Durbar for Edward VII; Lytton held the 1877 Durbar and Hardinge II the 1911 Durbar.

s: Which was the only Delhi Durbar attended by the monarch?
x: The 1911 Durbar, for George V and Queen Mary, was the only one attended by the monarch.

s: The Delhi Conspiracy Case of 1912 was associated with an attempt to assassinate
o: Lord Lytton during the 1877 Delhi Durbar
Lord Curzon during the 1905 Partition announcement
Lord Mayo during his tour of the Andamans
Lord Hardinge II during the state-entry procession into Delhi
x: In 1912, Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal attempted to assassinate Lord Hardinge II during his state-entry procession into Delhi.

s: In which year was the transfer of the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi announced?
x: The shift of the capital to Delhi was announced at the Delhi Durbar of 12 December 1911 under Hardinge II.

s: Which new province was announced at the Delhi Durbar of 1911 and formed in 1912?
x: On 12 December 1911 Bihar and Orissa was announced as a separate province, formed in 1912.

s: In which year was New Delhi inaugurated?
x: The capital shift was announced in 1911; New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931.

s: Who threw a bomb at Lord Hardinge II during his state entry into Delhi in 1912?
o: Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal
x: In the Delhi Conspiracy (1912), Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal threw a bomb at Hardinge II.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: The Indian Universities Act was passed in 1904 during Lord Curzon's tenure, not during Lord Lansdowne's tenure. The other three pairs are correctly matched.

s: Which Viceroy created the North-West Frontier Province?
x: The NWFP was formed under Curzon (1899-1905).

s: By what name was the anti-Partition movement that led to the revocation of the Partition of Bengal known?
x: The anti-partition Vande Mataram movement contributed to the revocation of the Partition of Bengal, which was announced through King George V in 1911.

s: On which date did the Partition of Bengal come into effect?
x: The Partition was announced on 20 July 1905 and took effect on 16 October 1905; it was annulled on 12 December 1911.

s: What is the motto of the Archaeological Survey of India?
x: The motto of the Archaeological Survey of India is 'Pratnakirti Apavarini'.

s: Under which Viceroy was the Archaeological Survey of India set up in 1861?
x: The ASI was set up in 1861 under Canning, with Cunningham as founder; Curzon later revived it.

s: Who was the first Archaeological Surveyor of India?
x: Alexander Cunningham was the first Archaeological Surveyor; John Marshall later became Director-General.

s: In which year did the Archaeological Survey become a separate department?
x: The Archaeological Survey became a separate department in 1871; Marshall took charge in 1902 and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act came in 1904.

s: In which year did John Marshall take charge as Director-General of the Archaeological Survey?
x: Curzon appointed John Marshall, who took charge in 1902.

s: The AMASR Act, 1958 protects monuments older than how many years?
x: The AMASR Act 1958 protects monuments over 100 years old.

s: Under which Viceroy was the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act passed in 1904?
x: Curzon passed the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 and reorganised the Department of Archaeology.

s: During whose viceroyalty was the Indian Universities Act of 1904 passed?
x: Curzon passed the Indian Universities Act in 1904, not Lansdowne; the first universities came in 1857 under Canning.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India.
2. Lord Mountbatten was the first Governor-General of free India.
3. C. Rajagopalachari was the first and the last Indian Governor-General.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and stayed on as the first Governor-General of independent India. C. Rajagopalachari succeeded him as the only Indian to hold the office, which makes him both the first and the last Indian Governor-General. Options A, B and C each leave out at least one true statement.

s: Which Viceroy came immediately after Lord Minto II?
x: The order is Curzon, Minto II, Hardinge II, Chelmsford and Reading.

s: Who was the first and last Indian Governor-General?
x: C. Rajagopalachari (1948-50) was the first and last Indian Governor-General.

s: In which year was the August Offer made?
x: The August Offer was in 1940, between the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) and the Wavell Plan (1945).

s: Who among the following, with Cripps and A.V. Alexander, formed the Cabinet Mission of 1946?
x: The Cabinet Mission members were Cripps, A.V. Alexander and Pethick-Lawrence.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Chelmsford — Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh tragedy
x: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh (1919) came under Chelmsford; Quit India and the August Offer belong to Linlithgow, and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact to Irwin.

s: On which date was the Indian Independence Act, which abolished the offices of Viceroy and Secretary of State, passed?
x: The Indian Independence Act of 18 July 1947 abolished the offices of Viceroy and Secretary of State.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Lord Linlithgow is associated with the Second World War and the August Offer.
2. Lord Linlithgow is associated with the Cripps Mission and Quit India.
3. Lord Wavell is associated with the First Afghan War.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
x: Linlithgow saw the Second World War, the August Offer, the Cripps Mission and Quit India; the First Afghan War belongs to Lord Auckland, not Wavell.

s: To whose viceroyalty do Chauri Chaura and the Swaraj Party belong?
x: Reading is linked with Chauri Chaura and the Swaraj Party; Irwin with the Simon Commission and Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

s: Which Viceroy is correctly matched with his tenure?
x: Willingdon served 1931–1936; Irwin served 1926–1931, Linlithgow from 1936 and Wavell from the mid-1940s to 1947.

s: Whose memoir is 'The Viceroy's Journal'?
x: 'The Viceroy's Journal' is Wavell's memoir.

s: To whose viceroyalty do the Communal Award and the Poona Pact belong?
x: Willingdon (1931-36) saw the Communal Award and the Poona Pact; Irwin saw the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

s: In which year did the Wavell Plan and the Simla Conference fail?
x: The Wavell Plan and Simla Conference (1945) failed on Jinnah's stand.

s: On which date did Attlee make the statement after which Mountbatten replaced Wavell?
x: Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947 led to Mountbatten replacing Wavell; 18 July 1947 is the date of the Indian Independence Act.

s: During whose viceroyalty was the Simon Commission appointed?
x: The Simon Commission came during the viceroyalty of Irwin (1926-31).

s: During whose tenure was the Indian Councils Act of 1892 passed?
x: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was passed during Lord Lansdowne's tenure.

s: During whose viceroyalty were Rand and Ayerst killed by the Chapekar brothers (1897)?
x: The killing of Rand and Ayerst in 1897 happened under Elgin II, during the famine and plague of 1896-97.

s: During whose viceroyalty did the Munda uprising (1899) take place?
x: The Munda uprising of 1899 came at the end of Elgin II's term (1894-99).

s: Who were the first Telugu political prisoners referred to in connection with 18 July 1908?
o: Alluri Sitarama Raju and Tanguturi Prakasam
x: Gadicherla and Bodi Narayana Rao are identified as the first Telugu political prisoners on 18 July 1908, during Minto II's tenure.

s: During whose viceroyalty were separate electorates introduced by the Indian Councils Act, 1909?
x: The Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) under Minto II introduced separate electorates.

s: Under the Indian Councils Act, 1861, for how long at most could an Ordinance issued by the Governor-General last?
x: The 1861 Act let the Governor-General issue Ordinances lasting up to six months.

s: Who divided revenue heads into imperial, provincial and divided heads in 1882?
x: Ripon (1882) divided revenue heads into imperial, provincial and divided; Lytton had widened the provincial heads in 1877.

s:
Consider the following statements about financial decentralisation:
1. Under Mayo, provinces got fixed annual grants for police, jails, education, medical services and roads.
2. Provinces could raise local taxes to balance their budgets.
3. Lytton widened the provincial heads in 1877.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: Mayo gave fixed grants and power to raise local taxes, and Lytton widened the provincial heads in 1877.

s: With which subject did the Raleigh Commission deal?
x: Raleigh dealt with universities; Hunter with education, Durand with the Afghan boundary and Lyall with famine.

s: During whose viceroyalty were the Irrigation Commission of 1901, the Police Commission of 1902 and the Universities Commission of 1902 all appointed?
x: All three commissions were appointed during Lord Curzon's viceroyalty. Their chairmen or associations were Scott-Moncrieff, Andrew Frazer and Raleigh respectively.

s:
Which of the following correctly represents the sequence of the three Famine Commissions?
1. Strachey
2. Lyall
3. MacDonnell
x: The famine commission chain was Strachey under Lytton, Lyall under Elgin II and MacDonnell under Curzon.

s: Under which Viceroy was the Durand Commission (1893) on the Afghan boundary appointed?
x: The Durand Commission of 1893 belongs to Lansdowne's viceroyalty.

s: During whose viceroyalty was the Royal Commission on Labour (1929) appointed?
x: The Royal Commission on Labour (1929) belongs to Irwin's viceroyalty.

s: Who appointed the Strachey Famine Commission (1880)?
x: Lytton appointed the Strachey Famine Commission; Lyall was under Elgin II and MacDonnell under Curzon.

s: With which subject did the Scott-Moncrieff Commission (1901) deal?
x: The Scott-Moncrieff Commission (1901) under Curzon dealt with irrigation; the Frazer Commission dealt with police.

s: Which subject did the Hunter Commission (1882) examine?
x: The Hunter Commission of 1882, under Ripon, dealt with education.

s: Who headed the Select Committee appointed by Parliament in 1772 to inquire into Company affairs?
x: In 1772 Parliament appointed a Select Committee under Burgoyne along with a Secret Committee.

s: At what rate did Parliament cap the Company's dividend in 1767?
x: In 1767 Parliament capped the dividend at 10 per cent and made the Company pay £400,000 a year.

s: How much was the Company made to pay the state every year for its territorial revenues in 1767?
x: The 1767 terms required the Company to pay £400,000 a year to the state.

s: Besides the Select Committee, which body did Parliament appoint in 1772 to inquire into Company affairs?
x: In 1772 Parliament appointed a Select Committee (Burgoyne) and a Secret Committee; their reports led to the Regulating Act.

s: Who granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company in 1765?
x: After Buxar (1764), the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani to the Company in 1765.

s: In which year was the Battle of Buxar fought?
x: The Battle of Buxar was fought in 1764; the Diwani followed in 1765.

s: Which was the first step by the British Parliament to control the East India Company?
x: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first parliamentary measure to control the Company and recognised its political and administrative functions.

s: The Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) consisted of one Chief Justice and how many other judges?
x: It had one Chief Justice and three judges with civil and criminal jurisdiction.

s: Which one of the following statements about the Regulating Act of 1773 is NOT correct?
o: It provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
It abolished the Court of Directors of the Company.
It required the Court of Directors to report on revenue, civil and military affairs to the British Government.
It was the first step by the British Parliament to control the Company.
x: The Act did not abolish the Court of Directors (APPSC-GS 2019 'incorrect statement'). Instead it made the Directors report to the British Government on revenue, civil and military affairs. It also provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta, set up in 1774, and it was Parliament's first step to control the Company.

s: Under the Regulating Act, 1773, the Governor-General's council had how many members?
x: The Act gave the Governor-General a council of four: Philip Francis, Clavering, Monson and Barwell.

s: Which of the following was NOT a member of the Governor-General's council named in the Regulating Act?
x: Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court; the council was Francis, Clavering, Monson and Barwell.

s: Who was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta?
x: Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774).

s: Under the Regulating Act, 1773, the presidencies of Bombay and Madras were:
o: placed under the Board of Control
x: The Act made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General with supervisory powers and subordinated Bombay and Madras to Bengal.

s: Who was the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act, 1773?
x: The Regulating Act made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal, and Warren Hastings was the first to hold it.

s: Warren Hastings was repeatedly outvoted under the Regulating Act because the Governor-General had:
x: Decisions were by majority and the Governor-General had only a casting vote, so Francis, Clavering and Monson could outvote him.

s: Under the Regulating Act of 1773, the Governor-General:
o: could override his Council in special cases
had an unrestricted veto over his Council
could be outvoted by his Council
x: The Governor-General had no veto and could be outvoted by his Council; the override power came only with the Act of 1786.

s: In which year was the Supreme Court at Madras, serving British subjects in the Madras Presidency including Andhra, set up?
x: The Madras Supreme Court was set up in 1801; the Calcutta Supreme Court dates from 1774.

s: What did the Act of 1773 make the Governor of Bengal?
x: The 1773 Act created the Governor-General of Bengal and subordinated Bombay and Madras.

s: In which year was the Regulating Act passed?
x: The Regulating Act was passed in 1773; Pitt's India Act came in 1784, the Charter Act in 1813 and the Government of India Act in 1858.

s: Which Act remedied the Council–Court clashes caused by the Supreme Court's undefined jurisdiction?
x: The 1781 Act of Settlement exempted official acts and revenue from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Amending Act, 1781:
1. It exempted the Governor-General and Council from the Supreme Court for acts in their official capacity.
2. It excluded revenue matters from the Court's jurisdiction.
3. It created the Board of Control.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 1781 Act exempted official acts and excluded revenue matters; the Board of Control came with Pitt's India Act, 1784.

s: By what other name is the Amending Act of 1781 known?
x: The Amending Act of 1781 is called the Act of Settlement; it curbed the Supreme Court.

s: Which Act ended the 'Double Government' set up by Pitt's India Act (1784)?
x: Pitt's India Act created the dual system, which lasted until the Government of India Act of 1858.

s: The Board of Control under Pitt's India Act had up to how many commissioners?
x: The Board of Control had up to six commissioners, including a Secretary of State and the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

s: Under the dual system of Pitt's India Act, with whom did the Company's commercial affairs remain?
x: Commercial affairs stayed with the Court of Directors while political affairs went to the Board of Control.

s: Which of the following was a member of the Board of Control under Pitt's India Act, 1784?
o: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Calcutta
Chairman of the Court of Directors
x: The Board of Control had up to six commissioners, including a Secretary of State and the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

s: The Act of 1786 was passed to meet the condition of which Governor-General for accepting office?
x: The Act of 1786 met Cornwallis's condition, letting the GG override his Council and act as Commander-in-Chief.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Act of 1786?
o: It let the Governor-General override his Council in special cases
It remedied the repeated outvoting of the Governor-General by his Council
It was passed to meet Lord Cornwallis's condition for accepting office
It remedied the absence of a Board of Control
x: The Act of 1786 fixed the outvoting of the Governor-General by giving him an override power; the Board of Control had already been created by Pitt's India Act, 1784.

s: Besides the power to override his council, what else did the Act of 1786 make the Governor-General?
o: President of the Board of Control
x: The Act of 1786 let the Governor-General override his council and also be Commander-in-Chief.

s: To whom did the Charter Act of 1793 extend the overriding power?
x: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the overriding power to the governors of the presidencies.

s: In which year was Pitt's India Act passed?
x: The order was Regulating Act 1773, Amending Act 1781, Pitt's India Act 1784 and Act of 1786.

s: Which Act directed the Supreme Court at Calcutta to respect the personal laws of Hindus and Muslims?
x: The Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) required the Court to respect Hindu and Muslim personal laws and exempted official acts.

s: Which Act came between the Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784)?
x: The order is Regulating Act 1773, Amending Act 1781, Pitt's India Act 1784, Act of 1786.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Pitt's India Act (1784) set up the dual system; the Board of Control is 1784, the override power 1786 and the Act of Settlement 1781.

s: Which Charter Act first asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's Indian possessions?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's Indian possessions.

s: Which Charter Act officially allowed Christian missionaries to enter India?
x: Under Evangelical pressure (Wilberforce, Charles Grant), the Charter Act of 1813 allowed missionaries to enter and preach.

s: What was the annual education grant provided by the Charter Act of 1813?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 gave Rs 1,00,000 (1 lakh) a year for education. It was the first step towards State responsibility for education.

s: Along with William Wilberforce, who pressed for the entry of missionaries under the Charter Act of 1813?
x: William Wilberforce and Charles Grant led the Evangelical pressure that got missionaries admitted in 1813.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1813:
1. It provided an education grant of Rs 10 lakh a year.
2. It allowed missionaries to enter India and preach.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 1813 grant was Rs 1 lakh a year, not Rs 10 lakh; missionaries were allowed to enter and preach.

s: To which Act does the Ministry of Law and Justice, the oldest organ of the Government of India, trace its origin?
x: The Ministry traces its origin to the Charter Act of 1833, which introduced the Law Member and the first Law Commission.

s: By which Act was the Company's exclusive right to trade in tea and with China abolished?
x: The Charter Act of 1833 removed the Company's remaining monopoly over tea trade and trade with China.

s: Which of the following is correct about the Charter Act of 1833?
o: It was the first Charter Act to renew the Company's authority for a fixed 20-year term.
It abolished the Governor-General's office without creating a successor.
It was the final step towards centralisation and made the Company purely administrative.
It restored the law-making powers of the presidencies.
x: The Charter Act of 1833 is regarded as the final step towards centralisation and converted the Company into a purely administrative body.

s: Which Charter Act ended the Company's commercial functions and made it a purely administrative body?
x: The 1833 Act ended the Company's commercial rights, leaving it purely administrative, and let Europeans settle freely.

s: Which Charter Act allowed Europeans to settle freely in India?
x: The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company's commercial rights and let Europeans settle freely in India.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1833, what were the laws made by the Governor-General-in-Council called?
x: From 1833 laws were called Acts instead of Regulations, and legislative power for all British India went to the GG-in-Council.

s: Who was the first Law Member (the fourth member) of the Governor-General's Council under the Charter Act of 1833?
x: The 1833 Act added a Law Member as the fourth member of the Council; T. B. Macaulay was the first to hold the post.

s: On which grounds did Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 say that no Indian should be barred from office?
o: Province, gender, tribe or political opinion
Religion, place of birth, descent or colour
x: Section 87 declared that religion, place of birth, descent or colour should not bar an Indian from holding office.

s: In 1836, what was the territory of the Agra Presidency, separated from Bengal under the Charter Act of 1833, renamed as?
x: The separated territory was placed under the Agra Presidency in 1834 and renamed the North-Western Provinces in 1836.

s: Who was the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833?
x: The 1833 Act made the GG of Bengal the GG of India; Lord William Bentinck was the first, and also the last GG of Bengal.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1833, the Law Member was added to the Governor-General's Council as which member?
x: The Law Member was the fourth member of the Council; the Act did not provide for an Indian Law Member.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Charter Act of 1833?
o: The Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India
Laws made by the Governor-General-in-Council were called Acts
It provided for an Indian Law Member
The Presidencies lost their law-making powers
x: The 1833 Act added a Law Member (Macaulay) but did not provide for an Indian Law Member.

s: Who was the last Governor-General of Bengal and the first Governor-General of India?
x: Under the Charter Act of 1833, Lord William Bentinck, the last GG of Bengal, became the first GG of India.

s: Who chaired the first Law Commission (1834) which drafted the Indian Penal Code?
x: The first Law Commission was set up in 1834 under Macaulay and drafted the IPC.

s: In the debate on which Act did Macaulay say, "The Company is an anomaly but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly"?
x: Macaulay made this observation in his speech in the House of Commons on the Bill that became the Charter Act of 1833.

s: During which period did the First Law Commission headed by Macaulay function?
x: Macaulay headed the First Law Commission (1834–38), which drafted the Indian Penal Code.

s: Which Act is called the 'final step towards centralisation', giving the Governor-General-in-Council exclusive legislative power?
x: The Charter Act of 1833 gave the GG-in-Council exclusive legislative power for all British India, the peak of centralisation.

s: Which Charter Act renewed the Company's authority with no fixed term?
x: The Charter Act of 1853, the last one, renewed the Company's authority without fixing a term.

s: Which was the last Charter Act of the East India Company?
x: The Charter Act of 1853 was the last; the Government of India Act of 1858 then transferred authority to the Crown.

s: Which Act said that the Indian territories of the East India Company were held "in trust" for the Crown?
x:
APPSC 2018 and the app: Charter Act 1853. Laxmikanth and PMF also give the 'in trust' clause in the Charter Act 1833 (Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28).
The Charter Act of 1853 renewed the Company's rule with no fixed term, the territories being held 'in trust for Her Majesty' until Parliament provided otherwise. The 1833 Act already used the words 'in trust for His Majesty'.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Charter Act of 1853?
o: Four members were appointed by Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra, the first local representation.
Six new legislative members were added.
The new members formed a separate Central Legislative Council.
The other two new legislative members were the Commander-in-Chief and the Law Member.
x: The two remaining members were not the Commander-in-Chief and the Law Member; they included the Chief Justice.

s: In which year was the Macaulay Committee on the Indian Civil Service constituted?
x: The Macaulay Committee (1854) recommended competitive examinations in place of nomination and favoured graduates.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, how many new legislative members were added to the Governor-General's Council?
x: Six legislative members were added, making a Central Legislative Council of 12 members in all.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, besides four provincial members and one Calcutta Supreme Court judge, who was among the new legislative members?
x: The six were four provincial appointees, the Chief Justice and one Supreme Court judge; the Commander-in-Chief was not among them.

s: How is the Central Legislative Council created by the Charter Act of 1853 often described?
x: With legislative functions separated and provincial members added, the 1853 Council worked as a 'mini-Parliament'.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, which province was represented along with Madras, Bombay and Bengal among the new legislative members?
x: The four provincial members came from Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1853, what replaced the patronage of the Directors in civil service appointments?
o: Nomination by the Board of Control
x: The Charter Act of 1853 ended the Directors' patronage and threw the civil services open to competitive examination.

s: Till which year did the Court of Directors make appointments to the Company's civil services?
x: The Directors appointed civil servants till 1853, when the Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act of 1853:
1. It separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.
2. It renewed the Company's charter for 20 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 1853 Act separated legislative from executive work, but renewed the Company's rule with no fixed term, not 20 years.

s: What did the Macaulay Committee of 1854 recommend for the Indian Civil Service?
o: Nomination by the Court of Directors
Competitive examinations instead of nomination, with preference for graduates
x: The Macaulay Committee (1854) recommended competitive exams in place of nomination and preferred graduates.

s: For how many years did the Charter Act of 1793 renew the Company's charter?
x: The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the charter and the trade monopoly for 20 years.

s: Under the Charter Act of 1793, from which source were the salaries of the Board of Control members paid?
x: The 1793 Act charged Board of Control members' salaries to Indian revenues.

s: In which year was Macaulay's Minute on Education written?
x: Macaulay's Minute on Education was issued in 1835.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Raja Ram Mohan Roy – demand for Indian participation in services, 1853
Charter Act of 1813 – open competitive examination for the ICS
Fort William College – established by Wellesley, 1806
x: Haileybury replaced Fort William College in 1806. Fort William College was set up in 1800, Roy's demand came in 1832 and open examinations came with the Charter Act of 1853.

s: Who first demanded the appointment of Indians in the services, in 1832?
x: Raja Ram Mohan Roy first demanded Indians in the services in 1832.

s: In which year did Haileybury replace Fort William College for training civil servants?
x: Fort William College (1800) gave way to Haileybury College in 1806.

s: Which of the following event–year pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: The Battle of Buxar was fought in 1764; 1757 is the year of Plassey.

s: Which Act reversed the centralising trend by restoring legislative power to Bombay and Madras?
x: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 restored law-making power to Bombay and Madras, beginning decentralisation.

s: Which Act created the Board of Control?
x: Pitt's India Act of 1784 set up the Board of Control; it was not created by any Charter Act.

s: Along with Thomas Munro, who is associated with the Ryotwari Settlement?
x: Ryotwari is linked to Thomas Munro and Alexander Read; the Permanent Settlement to Cornwallis.

s: Who extended the Ryotwari system in the Bombay Presidency?
x: Mountstuart Elphinstone extended Ryotwari in Bombay; Munro is linked with the Ceded Districts and Read with Baramahal.

s: Which of the following areas did NOT come under the Ryotwari system?
x: Ryotwari covered Madras, Bombay, Assam, Coorg, Berar and East Punjab; Bihar was under the Permanent Settlement.

s: What was the nature of the revenue assessment under the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems?
x: Revenue was fixed forever under the Permanent Settlement, but periodically revised under Ryotwari and Mahalwari.

s: In which year did Baramahal come under Company control after the Third Mysore War?
x: Baramahal came under the Company in 1792, before the Permanent Settlement was made permanent (1793).

s:
Assertion (A): Under the Ryotwari settlement, revenue was fixed on the land rather than directly on the crop produced.
Reason (R): Under the Ryotwari settlement, the assessment was ordinarily revised about every thirty years.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are features of Ryotwari, but periodic revision does not explain why revenue was fixed on land.

s: Which of the following was NOT identified as a major problem of the Ryotwari system?
o: Permanent fixing of revenue at a low and unchangeable rate
x: Ryotwari suffered from over-assessment, inadequate records and unclear boundaries. Its revenue was periodically revised and often heavy, not permanently fixed at a low rate.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the first Ryotwari experiment?
o: Alexander Read was assisted by Munro.
The initial demand was 30% of the estimated produce.
x: The first Ryotwari demand was 50% of the estimated produce, not 30%.

s: Under the Ryotwari system, which of the following rights was available to the ryot so long as the assessment was paid?
o: Only the right to cultivate, without transfer rights
The right to sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land
The right to remit all land revenue permanently
The right to collect revenue from other cultivators
x: The ryot held proprietary rights and could sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land as long as the assessment was paid.

s: Under the Ryotwari system, what happened to revenue after a bad harvest?
o: an automatic general exemption from revenue was granted
occasional remission or reduction of revenue was possible
x: Ryotwari gave no automatic exemption, but occasional remission or reduction was possible.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Ryotwari system:
1. Lands were surveyed and assessed before taxing.
2. The ryot could sell, mortgage or lease land while the assessment was paid.
3. Revenue was fixed permanently at a low rate.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Ryotwari lands were surveyed first and the ryot could sell or mortgage land; revenue was often heavy and periodically revised, not fixed low.

s: The first Ryotwari revenue demand was fixed at what share of the estimated produce?
x: The first Ryotwari demand was 50% of estimated produce, not 30%.

s: Who made the first Ryotwari experiment in Baramahal in 1792?
x: Captain Alexander Read began the Baramahal experiment in 1792, assisted by Munro.

s: In which year was the Ryotwari system generally adopted across the Madras Presidency?
x: General adoption in Madras came in 1820, with Munro as Governor.

s: Which of the following was NOT part of the Baramahal area?
x: Baramahal covered Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri and Tiruvannamalai; Anantapur was Munro's HQ in the Ceded Districts.

s: Under whom did Thomas Munro serve as assistant in the Baramahal?
x: Munro was Assistant to Read in the Baramahal, then Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, President of the Judicial Commission and Governor of Madras.

s: Against which system was the criticism made that the State became the 'ultimate landlord'?
x: Critics held that under Ryotwari the state became the ultimate landlord and its revenue was as heavy as zamindari rent.

s: In which region of Andhra did Thomas Munro first introduce the Ryotwari system in 1802?
x: Munro brought Ryotwari to the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) in 1802; the Northern Circars were mainly zamindari.

s: Which system did John Shore help Cornwallis to plan?
x: John Shore helped plan the Permanent Settlement; Ryotwari was linked to Read and Munro and Mahalwari to Holt Mackenzie.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Permanent Settlement?
o: It covered Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Varanasi.
It was associated with Lord Cornwallis.
Zamindars were recognised as proprietors of the land.
It was introduced in Madras and Coorg.
x: Madras and Coorg came under Ryotwari, not the Permanent Settlement.

s: In which year was the Permanent Settlement introduced in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa?
x: It was introduced in 1793 (not 1795), planned by Cornwallis with John Shore.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the land revenue system in the areas named?
x: Madras and Coorg came under Ryotwari, not the Permanent Settlement.

s: Who introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793?
x: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha in 1793, planned with John Shore.

s: Which of the following pairs (settlement – approximate share of British-held area) is correctly matched?
x: The Permanent Settlement covered about 19%, Ryotwari about 51% and Mahalwari about 30%, so Ryotwari and Mahalwari together covered about 81%.

s: Under the Sunset Law of the Permanent Settlement, when could an estate be auctioned?
o: the annual revenue was not paid by sunset on the due date
the tenant refused to accept a patta
the zamindar failed to improve the land within ten years
x: If the required revenue was not paid by sunset of the due date, the estate could be auctioned.

s: The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 dealt with which subject?
o: Auction of Zamindaris under the Sunset Clause
x: The Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants in Bengal and Bihar. Auction under the Sunset Clause belongs to the Permanent Settlement.

s: As which type of settlement did the Permanent Settlement begin?
x: It began as a ten-year (decennial) settlement and was later made permanent.

s: Under the zamindari system, to whom did the gains from agriculture mainly go?
x: Under the zamindari system, gains from agriculture went to the zamindars, not to the Company.

s: According to the commonly cited distribution of rent under the Permanent Settlement, what share was retained by the zamindar?
x: Under the Permanent Settlement the State took 10/11 of the rent collected and the zamindar kept 1/11.

s: Which of the following was NOT a rationale advanced for making the Permanent Settlement revenue demand fixed?
o: Ensuring that the Company would receive every future increase in agricultural prices
Reducing the cost of revenue collection
Securing an assured income for the Company
x: The rationale included assured income, lower collection costs, a loyal landlord class and the hope that zamindars would improve the land. A fixed demand actually prevented the Company from receiving additional revenue from later price increases.

s: Under the Permanent Settlement, what was the nature of the rights of zamindars?
x: Zamindars were recognised as proprietors with hereditary, transferable and saleable rights.

s: In which years were the Haftam and Panjam regulations, which let zamindars seize tenants' property, issued respectively?
x: Haftam came in 1799 and Panjam in 1812.

s: Which was a drawback of the fixed revenue demand of the Permanent Settlement for the Company?
o: It could not gain from later price rises
x: The fixed demand gave sure income at low cost but did not let the Company gain from later price rises.

s: To which of Cornwallis's measures was the rise in litigation after 1793 mainly traced?
x: More lawsuits after 1793 were traced to Cornwallis's judicial reforms, especially the abolition of court fees.

s: The sale of many old zamindari estates under the Permanent Settlement led to the rise of which class?
o: a new body of village karanams
a class of hereditary ryot proprietors in Madras
a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders
a class of Palegar intermediaries in Rayalaseema
x: Many old zamindars lost their estates for arrears, which were purchased by urban merchants and moneylenders, creating a new landed class.

s: Absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation and rack-renting were the effects of which settlement?
x: These, along with peasants reduced to tenants-at-will, were effects of the Permanent Settlement.

s: Under which Regulation did Holt Mackenzie propose the Mahalwari system in 1822?
x: Mackenzie's proposal came under Regulation VII of 1822; Regulation IX of 1833 was Bird's revision.

s: Which land revenue system was introduced in the North-Western Provinces (Agra-Oudh)?
x: The Mahalwari system, proposed by Holt Mackenzie in 1822, covered the North-Western Provinces, parts of Punjab and Central India.

s: Which of the following areas did NOT come under the Mahalwari system?
x: Madras was under the Ryotwari system; the Mahalwari system covered the North-Western Provinces, parts of Punjab, the Gangetic valley and Central India.

s: Under the Mahalwari system, who collected the revenue?
x: The lambardar collected under Mahalwari; the zamindar under the Permanent Settlement and the individual farmer under Ryotwari.

s: Under the Mahalwari system, what was the effect of a default in revenue payment?
o: the zamindar's estate liable to auction
x: Under Mahalwari the village was collectively liable; under Ryotwari the cultivator's land could be seized.

s: Under the Ryotwari system, after how many years was the revenue usually revised?
x: Ryotwari assessments were revised about every 30 years, unlike the permanently fixed zamindari demand.

s: Under the Permanent Settlement, who was the owner (proprietor) of the land?
x: The zamindar was the proprietor under the Permanent Settlement; the ryot under Ryotwari and the village jointly under Mahalwari.

s: Under the Mahalwari system, what was the unit of revenue assessment?
x: Under Mahalwari the mahal (village or estate) was the unit; revenue fixed for it was collected through the headman or village community.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Holt Mackenzie – devised the Mahalwari system
James Thomason – revised the system through a survey-based settlement
Holt Mackenzie – carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP
R.M. Bird – devised the Mahalwari system
x: Holt Mackenzie devised the Mahalwari system; R.M. Bird revised it through survey-based settlement and James Thomason carried on Bird's settlement.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Mahalwari system:
1. Its common ownership arrangement was called Bhai Chara.
2. Its common ownership arrangement was also called Mahali.
3. Its common ownership arrangement was called Peshkash.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Common ownership under the Mahalwari framework was called Bhai Chara or Mahali; Peshkash was the fixed payment of zamindars.

s: Who revised the Mahalwari system under Regulation IX of 1833 and is called the 'father of land settlement in north India'?
x: R.M. Bird revised the system in 1833 with a survey-based settlement.

s: Who carried on R.M. Bird's settlement in the North-Western Provinces as Lieutenant-Governor?
x: James Thomason continued Bird's settlement in the NWP.

s: With which region is the Taluqdari system associated?
x: Taluqdari belongs to Awadh (Oudh); 'Taluqdari – Bombay' is a wrong pair.

s: Into what did the three major British land revenue settlements turn land?
x: The settlements made land transferable, created a loyal landlord class and fed rural indebtedness and peasant revolts.

s: Which statement about village-lease settlements in the Ceded Districts is correct?
o: They replaced ryotwari after Munro left in 1808 and continued until ryotwari was restored around 1820.
They preceded the 1792 Baramahal experiment and ended in 1799.
They were introduced only in the Northern Circars and never in the Ceded Districts.
They permanently replaced all forms of direct settlement in Rayalaseema.
x: Village-lease settlements, in which village headmen acted as lessees, replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts after Munro's departure from 1808 onward and lasted until about 1820.

s: Where were Thomas Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts?
x: Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was at Anantapur.

s: Where was Sir Thomas Munro buried after he died of cholera at Pattikonda in 1827?
x: Munro died at Pattikonda (Kurnool) in 1827 and was buried at Gooty; Anantapur was his headquarters as Collector.

s: Which of the following best represents Thomas Munro's administrative philosophy?
o: Exclusive reliance on village headmen and moneylenders
Direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries and communication in fluent Telugu
Permanent fixation of revenue irrespective of local conditions
Indirect rule through zamindars and complete absence of official contact with cultivators
x: Munro favoured direct contact with cultivators, avoided intermediaries and was fluent in Telugu. He was also particularly fond of Rayalaseema.

s: Which post did Thomas Munro hold during 1814–18?
x: Munro was President of the Judicial Commission in 1814–18 and Governor of Madras in 1820–27.

s: By what title is Thomas Munro known?
o: Father of land settlement in north India
x: Munro, who spread Ryotwari across Madras as Governor, is called the 'Father of Ryotwari'; Bird is the father of land settlement in north India.

s: Who was the first Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts?
x: Thomas Munro was the first Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts (1800–07), with headquarters at Anantapur.

s: During which period was Thomas Munro the Governor of Madras?
x: Munro was Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827 and spread Ryotwari across the Presidency.

s:
Consider the following statements about Thomas Munro:
1. He was the Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827.
2. He was the President of the Judicial Commission before he became Governor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Munro headed the Judicial Commission (1814–18) and was then Governor of Madras (1820–27).

s: Why did Thomas Munro choose Rayalaseema for the Ryotwari system?
o: It had no strong zamindars and he distrusted palegars and big intermediaries
It already had the Permanent Settlement
It had the most irrigated land
x: Rayalaseema had no strong zamindars, and Munro distrusted palegars and intermediaries, so he settled directly with the ryots.

s: Who assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the Palegars in the Ceded Districts before the introduction of Ryotwari settlement?
x: Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer Campbell before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.

s: The Permanent Settlement introduced by Cornwallis in 1793 was implemented in Andhra in 1802 with which immediate effect?
o: The auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed
The zamindars were replaced by village headmen
Land revenue was remitted during every crop failure
All Zamindari estates were immediately abolished
x: In Andhra, Cornwallis's 1793 Act was implemented in 1802; it abolished the auction system and fixed the tax. Zamindari abolition occurred much later in 1948.

s: What did the zamindars of Coastal Andhra pay to the Company?
x: Coastal lands were divided into Haveli (direct Company control) and Zamindari areas, whose zamindars paid peshkash.

s: In which year was the Madras Inam Commission, which checked titles to rent-free inam lands, constituted?
x: The Madras Inam Commission was constituted in 1858 to investigate rent-free inam titles.

s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt in the 1840s is associated with which incident?
o: Defeating the Vizianagaram zamindar at Padmanabham
Introducing the Mahalwari system in Nellore
Obtaining the Northern Circars through a Mughal farman
Looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla
x: During the Kurnool Polygar revolt in the 1840s, Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy looted the treasury at Kovela Kuntla.

s: After 1802, Haveli lands were grouped into mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars. As what did the mootahdars generally hold them?
x: After 1802, mootahs were auctioned to mootahdars, who held them in the manner of proprietary estates. Many mootahdars later failed and fell into arrears.

s: Under which system were the Northern Circars mainly placed in the Madras Presidency?
x: The Northern Circars were mainly zamindari; Haveli lands under direct British control later came under Ryotwari.

s: Which legislation provided for the full conversion of Zamindari estates into Ryotwari holdings in the Madras Presidency?
o: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
x: The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 provided for the abolition of estates and their conversion into Ryotwari holdings.

s: In which year was the Permanent Settlement applied in the Circars and the Ryotwari system introduced in Rayalaseema?
x: These settlements came in 1802, after Guntur (1788), Padmanabham (1794) and the Ceded Districts (1800).

s: When did the Company obtain the Northern Circars?
x: The Northern Circars came in 1765–66 by Mughal farman and treaty with the Nizam; Guntur followed in 1788.

s: In which year did the Company acquire Guntur?
x: Guntur was acquired in 1788; the Ceded Districts came in 1800.

s: The Battle of Padmanabham (1794) saw the defeat of which Vizianagaram zamindar?
x: At Padmanabham in 1794 the Vizianagaram zamindar Vijayarama Gajapati Raju was defeated.

s: In the Andhra revenue system, on what was Moturpha levied?
x: Moturpha was levied on professions, trades and looms of weavers, artisans and merchants.

s: In the Andhra revenue system, what did 'Haveli' land mean?
x: Haveli was land under direct Company control; such lands were later brought under Ryotwari.

s: Under the mootah arrangement after 1802, what happened to many mootahdars?
x: Haveli lands grouped as mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars largely fell into arrears.

s: What was the Madras Inam Commission of 1858 set up to check?
x: The 1858 Inam Commission examined titles to rent-free inam lands.

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Acquisition of the Northern Circars by the Company
B. Cession of the Ceded Districts by the Nizam
C. Madras Inam Commission
D. Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Northern Circars 1765–66, Ceded Districts 1800, Inam Commission 1858 and the Estates Abolition Act 1948.

s: Why did rigid land revenue demands frequently push ryots towards moneylenders?
o: The government accepted revenue only in manufactured goods
Moneylenders alone were authorised to cultivate government land
Revenue had to be paid in cash even when crops failed
Ryots were prohibited from selling agricultural produce
x: The inflexible cash demand continued even during crop failures, forcing ryots to borrow from Mahajans and often mortgage or lose their land.

s: Which crops did the need to pay land revenue in cash encourage?
o: commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute
x: Cash revenue demands pushed peasants to grow commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute.

s: Which pairing of newly strengthened rural classes with the areas in which they emerged is correct?
o: Merchant-landlords — Zamindari areas; moneylender-landlords — Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas
Moneylender-landlords — Zamindari areas; merchant-landlords — Ryotwari areas only
Artisan-landlords — all areas; merchants — no rural areas
Village headmen — Zamindari areas; zamindars — Ryotwari areas only
x: Merchant-landlords became prominent in Zamindari areas, while moneylender-landlords emerged particularly in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.

s: On what ground did Alice Thorner criticise the Ryotwari system?
o: abolished all direct contact between the state and zamindars
created a permanent landlord class in the Northern Circars
made the village community the sole unit of settlement
destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government
x: Alice Thorner argued that Ryotwari destroyed the village system and isolated individual farmers from the government.

s: Which war was followed by the cotton slump that led to defaults and loss of land to moneylenders?
x: The cotton slump after the American Civil War led to defaults and land passing to moneylenders.

s: Which new class emerged in the Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas?
x: Moneylender-landlords rose in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas; merchant-landlords in zamindari areas.

s:
Consider the following statements about land revenue in Andhra:
1. The Mahalwari-type arrangement is associated with Nellore.
2. The Mahalwari-type arrangement is associated with Vizianagaram and Bobbili.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Nellore had a Mahalwari-type arrangement, where village headmen collected and paid the tax. Vizianagaram and Bobbili were zamindaris under the Permanent Settlement, paying peshkash.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the land-revenue pattern in Andhra?
o: Ryotwari in the Circars, Zamindari in the Ceded Districts and Mahalwari in Nellore
Mahalwari in the Circars, Zamindari in Rayalaseema and Ryotwari in Nellore
Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and Mahalwari in Nellore
Ryotwari in the Circars, Mahalwari in Rayalaseema and Zamindari in Nellore
x: The Andhra pattern was Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and a Mahalwari-type arrangement in Nellore.

s: In which book did R.P. Dutt set out the stages of colonialism?
o: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
x: R.P. Dutt proposed the three stages in India Today; Economic History of India is by R.C. Dutt.

s: For what did the Moderates' economic critique of colonialism become an important base?
o: The Swadeshi movement and early nationalism
The expansion of Company trade monopoly
x: The drain theory and the wider economic critique were major contributions of the Moderates and helped provide the basis for Swadeshi and early nationalism.

s: Who popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory in colonial India?
x: Dadabhai Naoroji popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory and was known as the Grand Old Man and the father of Indian Nationalism.

s: In which work did Dadabhai Naoroji first state the drain argument?
x: Naoroji first stated the drain in 'England's Debt to India' (1867); 'Economic History of India' is R.C. Dutt's.

s: Which newspaper and organisation are associated with Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti in the context of famine-related criticism in Andhra?
o: The Crescent and Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam
The Hindu and Madras Mahajana Sabha
Amrita Bazar Patrika and Indian Association
x: Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti reported Andhra famines in his paper The Crescent and founded the Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: R.C. Dutt — Economic History of India
William Digby — Essays on Indian Economics
G. Subramania Iyer — Economic History of India
x: R.C. Dutt wrote Economic History of India in two volumes. Prosperous British India was written by William Digby, while Essays on Indian Economics was associated with M.G. Ranade.

s: Which pair of author and book is correctly matched?
o: M.G. Ranade – Economic History of India
R.C. Dutt – Essays on Indian Economics
x: Digby wrote 'Prosperous' British India (1901); Ranade wrote Essays on Indian Economics and R.C. Dutt Economic History of India.

s: Who is the author of 'Some Economic Aspects of British Rule in India' (1903)?
x: G. Subramania Iyer wrote it in 1903, presenting India as a supplier of cheap raw materials.

s: Who coined the term 'moral drain'?
x: Dadabhai Naoroji coined 'moral drain'.

s: Who wrote the book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901)?
x: Dadabhai Naoroji wrote Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901).

s: Who is the author of 'Economic History of India' (1901–03)?
x: R.C. Dutt wrote the two-volume Economic History of India; R.P. Dutt wrote India Today.

s: What was India's per capita income in 1867–68 as first estimated by Dadabhai Naoroji?
x: Dadabhai Naoroji first estimated India's per capita income at Rs 20 for 1867–68.

s: Who is known as the 'Grand Old Man of India'?
x: Dadabhai Naoroji, the leading drain theorist, is called the 'Grand Old Man' and 'father of Indian Nationalism'.

s: Who is the author of 'Essays on Indian Economics'?
x: M.G. Ranade wrote 'Essays on Indian Economics' and founded the Indian school of economics.

s: Who is the author of 'Poverty of India: Papers and Statistics'?
x: 'Poverty of India: Papers and Statistics' grew out of Dadabhai Naoroji's 1876 paper 'The Poverty of India'.

s: Which of the following best describes the Drain of Wealth from India?
o: Transfer of Indian wealth to England without an adequate economic or material return
Movement of Indian capital from agriculture to indigenous industries
Exchange of Indian primary goods for British capital goods on equal terms
Import of British gold and silver into Indian markets
x: The Drain represented the transfer of India's wealth to England without a corresponding economic or material return.

s: What did the Moderates demand in response to the drain of wealth?
x: The Moderates demanded cuts in military spending, lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax and protective tariffs.

s: The interest part of the drain of wealth was interest on public debt raised where?
x: The interest was on public debt raised in Britain, not on loans from Indian peasants.

s: With which event is the Drain of Wealth from India considered to have begun?
x: The drain is traced to the grant of the Diwani of Bengal in 1765, after which Indian resources were transferred to England without economic return.

s: What rate of return was guaranteed to British investors in Indian railways?
x: Railway investors were guaranteed 5% whether or not the lines earned.

s: Which of the following was identified as a reason for the Drain of Wealth in the context of British colonial rule?
o: Excess imports of gold into India
Rapid growth of Indian-owned heavy industries
Profits taken by British capitalists from India
High domestic savings by Indian peasants
x: Profits taken by British capitalists from India were a recognised reason for the drain. An excess of imports was not the stated explanation.

s: What was India's export surplus mainly used for under colonial rule?
o: bring gold and silver into India
meet British office and war expenses
x: The export surplus did not bring matching gold or silver; it financed British office and war expenses.

s: Which was the largest single head of the British Indian budget?
x: Military expenditure on the British Indian Army and imperial wars was the largest single budget head.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the drain of wealth?
o: It took the form of an excess of imports
India generally had a favourable balance of trade
It began with the Diwani of Bengal
x: The drain took the form of unrequited exports, not an excess of imports.

s: Who proposed the stages of colonialism as mercantile, industrial capital and finance capital?
o: Dadabhai Naoroji in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
Richard Strachey in the Famine Code
Arthur Cotton in an irrigation report
x: R.P. Dutt proposed the three-stage interpretation in India Today, drawing on Karl Marx.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the stages of colonialism in India?
o: The mercantilist stage (1757-1813) saw Company trade monopoly and direct plunder.
In the free-trade stage (1813-1858) India became a market for British goods and a source of raw materials.
The Charter Act of 1813 opened the free-trade stage.
x: The finance-capital stage began in 1858; 1813 opened the free-trade stage.

s: Which statement best expresses the economic transformation of India under colonial rule?
o: India retained its position as an autonomous industrial exporter throughout colonial rule.
India changed from a raw-material supplier into the leading exporter of manufactures.
India changed from a leading exporter of manufactures into a supplier of raw materials.
India became exclusively a financial centre without agricultural exports.
x: Colonial economic change involved the decline of India's manufacturing export position and its transformation into a supplier of raw materials.

s: Which period did the free trade (industrial capital) stage of colonialism in India cover?
x: R.P. Dutt's free-trade stage ran 1813–1858, after the mercantilist stage (1757–1813).

s: Which Act ended the Company's Indian trade monopoly and opened India to British machine-made goods?
x: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly and opened India to British machine-made goods.

s: What does the term "one-way free trade" mean in the context of Indian deindustrialisation?
o: Free export of Indian manufactures and prohibition of British imports
Low-duty entry of British goods into India while Indian goods faced heavy duties in Britain
Exclusive trade between Indian princely states
Equal tariff treatment for Indian and British manufactures
x: British goods entered India almost duty-free, whereas Indian manufactures faced heavy duties in Britain.

s: What was the purpose of the cotton excise duty imposed on Indian mill cloth during 1894–96?
o: promote the export of Indian handlooms to China
abolish all duties on Indian textiles
offset the import duty on British goods
x: The cotton excise duty of 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was imposed to offset the import duty and is a classic example of tariff policy.

s: In which year was the Suez Canal, which tightened British control over Indian trade, opened?
x: The Suez Canal opened in 1869.

s: Who said the British had 'inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons'?
x: The phrase is Karl Marx's.

s: Which of the following was NOT a cause of deindustrialisation in India?
o: Railways carrying British goods into the interior
British traders being denied special privileges
Transit and customs duties hurting indigenous trade
Artisans being forced to reveal trade secrets
x: British traders actually received special privileges, so that statement is false.

s: In which year did Lancashire cloth first reach Bengal?
x: Lancashire cloth came to Bengal in 1786; calicoes were displaced by 1793.

s: By 1850, India took what share of all British cotton exports?
x: After 1813's one-way free trade, India took one-fourth of British cotton exports by 1850.

s: Who gave the list of causes of Indian deindustrialisation that included transit duties and British privileges?
x: B.D. Basu listed the causes: trade policy, raw-material export, duties, British privileges and railways.

s: According to Paul Bairoch, what was India's share of world manufactures in 1750?
x: Bairoch estimated India's share of world manufactures at about 24.5% in 1750; it fell under 2% by 1900.

s: India's share of world manufactures fell to below which level by 1900, according to Paul Bairoch?
x: Bairoch's figures show India's share falling from about 24.5% in 1750 to under 2% by 1900, a sign of deindustrialisation.

s: What was the state of agriculture that went along with deindustrialisation in colonial India?
x: Indian industry declined through loss of markets while agriculture stayed stagnant with low productivity.

s: Where was India's first jute mill set up in 1855?
x: The first jute mill was set up at Rishra in Bengal in 1855.

s: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company, established in 1854, is associated with which person?
x: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was established in 1854 by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar.

s: On the eve of independence, where were the foreign-owned jute mills concentrated?
x: Indian-owned cotton mills were in Maharashtra and Gujarat, and foreign-owned jute mills in Bengal.

s: Where was the first, failed attempt at a cotton mill in India made in 1818?
x: Fort Gloster (Kolkata) in 1818 failed; the first successful mill came in Bombay in 1854.

s: In which year was TISCO incorporated?
x: TISCO was incorporated in 1907 at Jamshedpur.

s: Which of the following is correct about ownership of mills in colonial India?
o: Cotton and jute mills were both Indian-owned
Cotton mills were foreign-owned; jute mills Indian-owned
Cotton mills were Indian-owned; jute mills foreign-owned
x: Cotton mills (Maharashtra, Gujarat) were Indian-owned; jute mills (Bengal) were foreign-owned.

s: Which was the first tea company in India, formed in 1839?
x: The Assam Company, formed in England in 1839 with Rs 5 lakh, was the first tea company; its headquarters was at Nazira.

s: At what rate did the Hilton Young Commission (1926) fix the rupee?
x: It fixed the rupee at 1s 6d; Indian business wanted 1s 4d. Its central bank proposal led to the RBI (1935).

s: Why did the higher rupee-sterling ratio (1s 6d) hurt Indian exporters?
o: made British imports dearer in India
x: A higher ratio made Indian goods dearer abroad; it also made British imports cheaper, a separate effect.

s: Against the Hilton Young ratio of 1s 6d, at what rate did Indian business led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas want the rupee?
x: Indian business wanted 1s 4d; the Commission fixed 1s 6d.

s: The Hilton Young Commission recommended a central bank. In which year was the RBI set up?
x: Its central-bank proposal led to the Reserve Bank of India in 1935.

s: On the eve of independence, agriculture employed over 75% of the workforce. What share of GDP did it contribute?
x: Agriculture employed over 75% of workers but gave only about 50% of GDP, showing low productivity.

s: What was the life expectancy in India on the eve of independence?
x: Per capita income was about Rs 265, life expectancy 32 years and literacy below 16%.

s: Which of the following received top priority in the First Plan in response to the immediate economic challenges after independence?
o: Heavy engineering, automobiles and export subsidies
x: Large foodgrain imports and inflation after independence led the First Plan to give top priority to agriculture, irrigation and power.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Basic and capital goods — approximately one-fourth of industrial output
Suez Canal — tightened British control over trade
Public sector before independence — steel, automobiles and aviation as its principal areas
x: Before independence, the public sector was limited mainly to railways, power, communications and ports. It did not principally cover all the industries listed in option d.

s: According to Angus Maddison, how did India's share of world income change from 1700 to 1950?
x: Maddison's estimate (APPSC-GS 2024 key) is that India's share of world income fell from about 27% in 1700 to about 3% in 1950, reflecting deindustrialisation and drain. The reversed pair (3% to 27%) is wrong, and 50%/10% and 15%/7% are not the cited figures.

s: What was the per capita income of India in 1947?
x: Per capita income on the eve of independence was about Rs 265 a year; Rs 20 was Naoroji's 1867–68 estimate.

s: What was the literacy rate in India on the eve of independence?
x: Literacy was under 16% (female under 9%); 32 years was life expectancy.

s: On the eve of independence, basic and capital goods formed about what share of industrial output?
x: India lacked a capital-goods base: basic and capital goods were only about one-fourth of industrial output.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India had a strong industrial base before British rule.
2. Deindustrialisation in India was a result of British policy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: India had a strong industrial base before British rule, and British trade policy caused its deindustrialisation.

s: Where did the Dutch set up their first factory in Andhra?
x: The Dutch set up their first Andhra factory at Machilipatnam, famous for chintz, dyed fabrics and muslins.

s: Which of the following pairs (place – product) is correctly matched?
x: Srikakulam was known for muslin; Machilipatnam for dyed clothes, Nellore for towels and Eluru for carpets.

s: In which district is Ponduru, known for fine hand-spun khadi, located?
x: Ponduru is associated with Srikakulam; Uppada is known for jamdani silk.

s: For which product is Uppada famous?
x: Uppada is known for jamdani silk; Eluru for carpets, Kurnool for blankets, Nellore for towels.

s: Which of the following place–product pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Ponduru is known for fine hand-spun khadi, not iron and steel.

s: What was the famous painted cloth of Machilipatnam in the 16th–17th centuries?
x: Machilipatnam was famed for chintz (painted cloth), dyed fabrics and muslins.

s: In British-period Andhra, which sector was the second-largest employer after agriculture?
x: Textiles gave the most jobs after agriculture in Andhra during British rule.

s: Why did the textile exports from Andhra ports such as Machilipatnam, Kakinada and Bhimunipatnam decline?
o: High duties imposed by the Company
A ban imposed by the Nizam
Failure of the cotton crop in famines
x: Under high Company duties the cloth trade of these ports to England, France and Holland shrank to small boats carrying salt and grain.

s: For which textile product was Nellore known in British-period Andhra?
x: Nellore was known for towels; Eluru for carpets, Kurnool for blankets and Srikakulam for muslin.

s: Which one of the following statements about early industrialisation in Andhra Pradesh is NOT correctly matched?
x: Ponduru was associated with Andhra textiles, not an iron and steel plant. Chittivalasa and Nellimarla had jute mills, while Rajahmundry had a paper mill.

s: Between which places was the first railway line in the Andhra region opened?
x: The first railway was the Puttur-Renigunta line, opened in 1862.

s: In which mineral did Visakhapatnam district lead the world in production during 1892–1929?
x: The manganese mines of Visakhapatnam district (Vizianagaram) made it the world leader in manganese from 1892 to 1929.

s: In colonial Andhra, which district was known for mica?
x: Mica was found in Nellore district, while Visakhapatnam district led the world in manganese.

s: Under the Tinkathiya system, on what part of each holding did indigo have to be grown?
x: Tinkathiya required indigo on 3/20 of each holding.

s: Which of the following pairs (crop – main region) is correctly matched?
x: Jute was grown mainly in Bengal; cotton in the Deccan, Gujarat and Berar, opium in Bengal-Bihar and Malwa, and tea in Assam.

s: In the triangular trade between India, China and Britain, what did India send to China?
x: Indian opium went to China, Chinese tea and silver to Britain, and British manufactures to India.

s: Why did famines become frequent in areas of commercialised agriculture?
o: cash crops replaced food crops, reducing food security
x: Replacement of food crops by cash crops cut food security and made famines more frequent.

s: Which event was followed by the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879)?
x: The Act, protecting peasants against moneylenders, followed the Deccan riots of 1875.

s: Which was the main tea-growing region under British rule?
x: Tea was grown mainly in Assam; jute in Bengal, cotton in the Deccan, Gujarat and Berar.

s: The Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900 checked the transfer of land from agriculturists to whom?
x: The Act stopped land passing from agriculturists to non-agriculturists such as moneylenders.

s: Against whom did the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act of 1879 protect peasants?
x: It protected peasants against moneylenders after the Deccan riots of 1875.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Orissa Famine — West and central India, 1899–1900
x: The Chalisa famine of 1783-84 struck North India (Delhi, Awadh, Punjab). The other pairs are wrong: Doji Bara was 1791-92 in the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars (Bengal 1770 is the Great Bengal Famine); the 1943 Bengal famine is not the 'Great Famine' (that name belongs to 1876-78 and 1896-97); and the Orissa famine was 1865-66 (1899-1900 hit west and central India).

s: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the appointment of which commission?
x: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the Campbell Commission.

s: Under which Viceroy did the Great Famine of 1876-78, which affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay, occur?
x: The Great Famine of 1876-78 occurred during Lytton's tenure.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Bengal Famine of 1943 — Bengal — Linlithgow and Wavell years
Great Famine of 1896–97 — Many parts of India — Elgin II
Great Bengal Famine of 1770 — Bengal — Lytton
Famine of 1899–1900 — West and Central India — Curzon
x: The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occurred under Cartier, not Lytton. The other pairs are correctly matched.

s: Which region was mainly affected by the Chalisa famine of 1783–84?
x: The Chalisa famine (1783–84), named after Vikram Samvat 1840, hit North India (Delhi, Awadh, Punjab).

s: Under whose governorship did the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occur?
x: The 1770 Bengal famine came under Cartier, when about a third of Bengal's people died; Lytton was the ruler of the 1876–78 Great Famine.

s: About how many people died in the Bengal famine of 1943?
x: About 30 lakh (3 million) people died in the 1943 Bengal famine, which led to the Woodhead Commission.

s: Which famine is known as the 'skull famine'?
x: The Doji Bara famine of 1791–92 in the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars is called the skull famine.

s: After which era is the Chalisa famine of 1783–84 named?
x: The Chalisa famine is named after the year 1840 of the Vikram Samvat.

s: About what share of Bengal's people died in the Great Bengal Famine of 1770?
x: About one-third of Bengal's people died in 1770, while the Company kept collecting revenue.

s: In which year did the Doji Bara famine occur?
x: Doji Bara was in 1791-92, between the Great Bengal Famine (1770) and the Orissa-Ganjam famine (1865-66).

s: The Guntur famine of 1832–33 led to the building of which work by Arthur Cotton?
x: The Guntur famine prompted Arthur Cotton's Godavari anicut (1847–52).

s: Which famine of 1833 gave the impetus for Cotton's Godavari anicut?
x: The Guntur famine of 1833 led to the construction of Cotton's Godavari anicut.

s: In which year was Arthur Cotton's Godavari anicut at Dowleswaram sanctioned?
x: It was reported in 1844, sanctioned in 1846, begun in 1847 and its main structure finished in April 1852.

s: Who proposed the Krishna anicut at Bezwada?
x: Colonel Henry Atlock Lake proposed the Krishna anicut at Bezwada.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: K.C. Canal — Sunkesula on the Tungabhadra — 1872
x: The Godavari anicut was at Dowleswaram, not Nellore. The Penna anicut was at Nellore in 1860, and the K.C. Canal dates from 1872 at Sunkesula on the Tungabhadra.
